query: We aim to synthesize an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy via ink-extrusion additive manufacturing using a precursor blend of metallic and hydride powders. The process relies on the sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) to drive alloying, where decomposition temperatures correlate with hydride formation enthalpies. To prevent the formation of alpha-HCP phases induced by dissolved oxygen (an alpha-stabilizer) which would otherwise degrade mechanical properties, the sintering atmosphere must be strictly controlled using an oxygen getter. The goal is to achieve a nearly fully dense microstructure where slow cooling results in a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure, but a rapid quench from the homogenization temperature traps a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure. Propose a hypothesis for the specific oxygen getter material and sintering regime that balances dehydrogenation kinetics with oxygen scavenging, predict the resulting phase constitution and grain size after rapid quenching, and design a falsification experiment using in-situ X-ray diffraction to verify the sequence of phase transformations and the absence of alpha-Ti during the critical decomposition window.

generation.hypothesis: Using a precursor blend of metallic and hydride powders (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) for ink-extrusion additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (driven by their formation enthalpies) will drive alloying. To prevent alpha-HCP phase formation induced by dissolved oxygen, an oxygen getter of excess ZrH2 (which decomposes at a lower temperature than TiH2 and HfH2, scavenging oxygen before the critical alloying window) combined with a sintering regime of 1350°C for 2 hours in a vacuum (<10^-4 Pa) followed by rapid water quenching from the homogenization temperature will yield a nearly fully dense microstructure. This regime balances dehydrogenation kinetics (ZrH2 decomposes ~400-500°C, TiH2 ~600-700°C, HfH2 ~800-900°C, NbH ~900-1000°C, TaH0.5 ~1000-1100°C) with oxygen scavenging. The rapid quench will trap a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure with a fine grain size (<10 μm), avoiding the dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure that would form under slow cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic blend of TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2 powders with excess ZrH2 as oxygen getter
generation.intervention: Ink-extrusion additive manufacturing followed by sintering at 1350°C for 2 hours in vacuum (<10^-4 Pa) and rapid water quenching from homogenization temperature
generation.conditions: Vacuum atmosphere (<10^-4 Pa), sintering temperature 1350°C, holding time 2 hours, rapid water quenching
generation.structural_mediator: Sequential hydride decomposition driven by formation enthalpies, with ZrH2 acting as oxygen getter
generation.mechanism: ZrH2 decomposes first, scavenging oxygen to prevent alpha-stabilizer formation; subsequent hydride decomposition drives alloying; rapid quenching suppresses alpha-BCC precipitation, trapping metastable beta-BCC
generation.predicted_outcome: Nearly fully dense microstructure with metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure and fine grain size (<10 μm)
generation.baseline: Slow cooling results in dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure with potential alpha-HCP formation due to oxygen
generation.boundary: Oxygen content must be <0.1 wt.%; hydride decomposition temperatures must be within 400-1100°C range; quenching rate must exceed critical cooling rate for beta-BCC retention
generation.uncertainty: Exact decomposition temperatures of hydrides in mixed powder environment may vary; oxygen getter efficiency depends on powder mixing homogeneity; rapid quenching may induce residual stresses
generation.falsification_experiment: In-situ X-ray diffraction during heating from 300°C to 1200°C at 10°C/min in vacuum to monitor hydride decomposition sequence and phase transformations. Verify absence of alpha-Ti peaks during the critical decomposition window (600-900°C) and confirm single-phase beta-BCC retention after rapid quenching. If alpha-Ti or alpha-HCP phases appear, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: XRD and SEM analysis showed that both the gravity-cast specimen and the suction-assisted cast specimen had one single NbTaTi-based BCC phase, while both materials were composed of a NbTaTi-based BCC phase and a ZrHf HCP phase in their HIP’ed condition. Having analyzed their XRD spectrum, Senkov at al. [ [3] ] pointed to the existence of a BCC phase in both the cast and the HIP’ed conditions. Though these researchers reported on a small peak at 2θ = 24.9° indicating the presence of a hexagonal-like phase, they did not refer to the six additional HCP peaks detected in the current study in the case of HIP gravity casting: 2θ = 31.95°, 2θ = 34.28°, 2θ = 37.34°, 2θ = 47.66°, 2θ = 56.79° and 2θ = 63.23°. Nor did they refer to the following six peaks in the case of the suction-assisted casting: 2θ = 32°, 2θ = 34.3°, 2θ = 36.4°, 2θ = 47.5°, 2θ = 57° and 2θ = 62.6°. As stated earlier, identification of the chemical composition of the two phases of the material in its HIP’ed state is based on combining EDS analysis of the two detected phases with the XRD results. Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.
